title: My day
verifiedBy: Fable (Claude Fable 5) — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: adhhab ilā al-madrasa runs in the order English expects: verb (with its person inside), "to", place. ilā sits exactly where "to" sits.

The verb of this module is the NON-PAST, and the person is a prefix: a- is I (adhhab, ashrab), ta- is you-m or she (tadhhab), ya- is he (yadhhab), na- is we (nadhhab). One form covers "I drink", "I am drinking" and "I do drink" — it is unmarked for time, which is why M6 can point it at tomorrow. One honest note: M1's uḥibb and urīd wear u- instead of a- because of their verb pattern, so your first two verbs are the exception, not the rule.
English needs "do" for the question and "-s" for he; Arabic has neither. hal tadhhab? is the question, and the prefix already did the person — nothing is added anywhere.
A habit is marked by a TIME word, never on the verb: kull yawm (every day), dāʾiman (always), aḥyānan (sometimes). The verb itself never changes for habit — ashrab al-qahwa kull yawm.

The time-of-day phrases are learned whole and written in full: fī aṣ-ṣabāḥ (in the morning), fī al-masāʾ (in the evening), fī al-layl (at night). Speech runs them together — fi ṣ-ṣabāḥ — but this course writes every letter. And ṣ is a sun letter, so it swallows the l of al-: aṣ-ṣabāḥ, the same law as M2's ash-shāy; m is a moon letter, so al-masāʾ keeps its l.
tashrab is BOTH "you drink" (to a man) AND "she drinks" — the same double duty M3's turīd had, on every ta- verb in the language.
yawm alone is "day"; with the article it becomes "today": al-yawm. It takes no preposition — al-yawm adhhab, not "fī al-yawm".
matā ("when") fronts the question the way kayfa did in M2, and the statement behind it does not move: matā tashrab al-qahwa? It replaces hal — a question can carry one question word, not two.

sentences.cue: I go to school every day

words.note: "Go", and the person is the prefix: adhhab (I), tadhhab (you-m / she), yadhhab (he), nadhhab (we) — and to a woman the ta- carries M3's -īn tail, tadhhabīn, exactly as turīdīn did. The a- is the regular first-person prefix that M1's u- verbs made you wait for. The dh is the th of "this".
"To", a separate little word sitting exactly where English puts it: adhhab ilā al-madrasa. It never glues onto the noun the way al- does.
madrasa is a school — the place of darasa, to study, and the same building M2's mudarris teaches in. Going to school in general keeps the article: ilā al-madrasa.

"Every day", learned as one piece, and it is what makes the sentence a habit — the verb itself never changes for that. kull is "every"; yawm is "day", a word al-yawm ("today") will bring back on its own.

sentences.trap: "I go" and "I am going" are the same Arabic word. The non-past is unmarked for time; kull yawm is what says this is a habit.
sentences.sound: ADH-hab i-LAA al-MAD-ra-sa kull YAWM — dh as in "this".

variations.cue: You go to school every day (to a man)
variations.changed: a- → ta-: the prefix is the whole change

variations.cue: He goes to school every day
variations.changed: a- → ya-: he, and no pronoun anywhere

variations.cue: You go to school every day (to a woman)
variations.changed: to a woman, ta- carries the -īn tail: tadhhabīn — turīdīn's law on a new verb

mistake.why: English "I go to school" is bare, so the article is easy to drop. Arabic keeps it: ilā al-madrasa. Bare madrasa is "a school", some school or other.

sentences.usage: The daily-routine sentence — swap the place and it carries your whole week.
sentences.mnemonic: madrasa — where darasa (study) happens; the mudarris from M2 works there.

sentences.cue: I drink coffee in the morning

words.note: "In the morning", learned whole. Inside it: ṣabāḥ is the morning of M2's ṣabāḥ al-khayr, and aṣ- is the article al- with its l swallowed by the sun letter ṣ — written as said, like ash-shāy. Speech elides the vowel — fi ṣ-ṣabāḥ — but the writing keeps every letter.

sentences.trap: The habit keeps M1's article: coffee in general is al-qahwa, even inside a morning routine.
sentences.sound: ASH-rab al-QAH-wa fi ṣ-ṣa-BAAḤ — said, the fī melts into the article.

variations.cue: I drink tea in the morning
variations.changed: swap the drink — the frame holds still

variations.cue: We drink coffee in the morning
variations.changed: a- → na-: we — the prefix does it all

variations.cue: Do you drink coffee in the morning? (to a man)
variations.changed: hal turns the habit into a question — the ta- already holds the you

mistake.why: ṣ is a sun letter, so the l of al- never survives in front of it. It is aṣ-ṣabāḥ — said that way and, in this course, written that way.

sentences.usage: Morning routines. The evening twin is fī al-masāʾ, at the end of the module.
sentences.mnemonic: ṣabāḥ you already greet with — ṣabāḥ al-khayr is this word plus goodness.

words.note: "Eat": ākul (I), taʾkul (you-m / she), yaʾkul (he). The long ā at the front is the a- prefix fused onto a verb that itself starts with a catch in the throat — which is also why the other persons carry a written ʾ in the middle.
fākiha is fruit; eating fruit in general keeps the article — ākul al-fākiha — exactly as uḥibb al-qahwa did in M1. English "I eat fruit" is bare; the Arabic habit is not.

sentences.trap: A habit is a statement about the whole class of thing, so M1's law applies: al-fākiha, article on.
sentences.sound: AA-kul al-FAA-ki-ha — the first syllable is long, aa.

variations.cue: You eat fruit every day (to a man)
variations.changed: ā- → taʾ-: you, with the little catch written

variations.cue: I eat fruit in the morning
variations.changed: every day → in the morning: swap one time word for another

variations.cue: He eats fruit every day
variations.changed: taʾ- → yaʾ-: he — the written catch stays, only the person letter moves

mistake.why: Bare fākiha is "a piece of fruit". The habit — fruit as a class — keeps the article English drops: ākul al-fākiha.

sentences.usage: Food habits. The verb will meet its past self (akaltu) in M5.
sentences.mnemonic: fākiha — fruit; the fruit bowl is the fākiha bowl.

words.note: M3's ashrab with the person changed: ya- is he, ta- is you-m or she, na- is we. Same stem, different front — the whole non-past paradigm in one word family.
"Always", with the adverb tail -an written out (like shukran, kathīran) and a written ʾ in its middle. Its everyday seat is the end of the sentence: yashrab ash-shāy dāʾiman.

sentences.trap: English tucks "always" before the verb; the Arabic adverb's everyday seat is the end of the sentence.
sentences.sound: YASH-rab ash-SHAAY DAA-ʾi-man — a tiny catch in the middle of dāʾiman.

variations.cue: You always drink tea (to a man)
variations.changed: ya- → ta-: you (or she — the double duty below)

variations.cue: He always drinks coffee
variations.changed: swap the drink — dāʾiman keeps its seat

variations.cue: He doesn't drink coffee
variations.changed: lā in front of the verb: the habit denied — dāʾiman would have nothing true to say

mistake.why: The English order — "always drinks tea" — imported whole. The everyday seat of dāʾiman is after the object, at the end: yashrab ash-shāy dāʾiman.

sentences.usage: Talking about someone else's habits — no pronoun needed, the ya- carries him.

words.note: "Sometimes" — literally "at times", plural of ḥīn (a time) — wearing the same written -an tail as dāʾiman, and sitting in the same end-of-sentence seat.

sentences.trap: tashrab here is SHE — the same shape that asks a man "do you drink?". Only the situation says which; M3's turīd taught the same collision.

variations.cue: She drinks milk every day
variations.changed: sometimes → every day

variations.cue: I sometimes drink milk
variations.changed: ta- → a-: back to I

variations.cue: We sometimes drink milk
variations.changed: ta- → na-: we — and only the prefix says so

mistake.why: For "she drinks", the prefix is ta-, not ya-: tashrab al-ḥalīb. yashrab says "he" — the ya-/ta- split is exactly where English "he/she drinks" splits, but on the front of the verb.

sentences.usage: Halfway habits — aḥyānan softens any routine sentence.
sentences.mnemonic: aḥyānan — "at times": ḥīn is a time, aḥyān is times.

sentences.cue: I go to work in the morning

words.note: ʿamal is work — the thing and the place you go to. Going to work in general keeps the article, like al-madrasa: ilā al-ʿamal. The ʿ opens the word from deep in the throat.

sentences.trap: Same trap as school: English "go to work" is bare, Arabic keeps the article — ilā al-ʿamal.

variations.cue: You go to work in the morning (to a man)
variations.changed: a- → ta-: you

variations.cue: I go to work every day
variations.changed: in the morning → every day

variations.cue: When do you go to work? (to a man)
variations.changed: matā fronts the question and the statement behind it does not move

mistake.why: English "go to work" carries no article, so it is the easiest one to drop. Arabic keeps it: ilā al-ʿamal.

sentences.usage: The commute sentence. Work or school — the frame is one frame.
sentences.mnemonic: ʿamal is work — and ʿamila, he worked, is where M5's suffix game will not go: this one stays daily.

sentences.cue: When do you drink coffee? (to a man)

words.note: "When", and it fronts the question the way kayfa did in M2: matā tashrab? Nothing behind it moves, and there is no "do" — the ta- already holds the you. It replaces hal: one question word per question.

sentences.trap: English builds "when DO you…"; Arabic puts matā in front of the plain statement and is done.
sentences.sound: MA-taa TASH-rab al-QAH-wa — the voice falls at the end; matā already marked the question.

variations.cue: When do you drink tea? (to a man)
variations.changed: swap the drink

variations.cue: When does he drink coffee?
variations.changed: ta- → ya-: he, and matā stays put

variations.cue: I drink coffee at night (the answer)
variations.changed: the answer: matā falls away and a time phrase takes its seat

mistake.why: An English "when do you…" has two question pieces, so both get imported. Arabic takes one: matā does the whole job, and hal only ever marks yes/no questions.

sentences.usage: Asking about anyone's routine. The answer is a time word: fī aṣ-ṣabāḥ.

sentences.cue: Today I am going to work

words.note: Two jobs in one row: yawm alone is "day" (kull yawm, every day), and with its article it is "today" — al-yawm, literally "the day". It needs no preposition: al-yawm adhhab, never fī al-yawm.

sentences.trap: The same verb that said "I go (every day)" says "I am going (today)". The non-past is unmarked; the time word decides.

variations.cue: Today I am going to school
variations.changed: work → school

variations.cue: Today you are going to work (to a man)
variations.changed: a- → ta-: you

variations.cue: I am going to work today
variations.changed: al-yawm moves to the end of the sentence — either seat is fine, and it still takes no preposition

mistake.why: English says "ON this day", so a preposition wants in. al-yawm stands alone: al-yawm adhhab.

sentences.usage: Today's plan, said in the plain non-past — no special tense needed.
sentences.mnemonic: al-yawm — THE day, the one you are standing in: today.

sentences.cue: Do you drink coffee at night? (to a man)

words.note: "At night", learned whole like its daytime siblings. layl is night; and because the article stands before a word that itself begins with l, the assimilation M2 taught changes nothing you can see — al-layl looks regular and is said with one long doubled l.

sentences.trap: hal + the plain statement, exactly as in M2 — English's "do" still has nowhere to go.
sentences.sound: hal TASH-rab al-QAH-wa fi l-LAYL — one long l where the article meets the night.

variations.cue: Do you drink tea in the evening? (to a man)
variations.changed: night → evening, coffee → tea

variations.cue: No, I drink water at night
variations.changed: the answer: lā, then the true habit

variations.display: lā, lā ashrab al-qahwa fī al-layl
variations.script: لا، لا أشرب القهوة في الليل
variations.cue: No, I don't drink coffee at night
variations.changed: two lā, two jobs: the answer no, then the not on the verb

mistake.why: English "at night" is bare, so the article slips off. The phrase keeps it: fī al-layl.

sentences.usage: Habits by time of day — and a genuinely useful question about caffeine.
sentences.mnemonic: layl — night; Laylā is the night-born name the famous love story is about.

sentences.cue: We drink tea in the evening

words.note: "In the evening", learned whole. masāʾ is the evening of masāʾ al-khayr (M2's variation), ending on a written hamza like māʾ. m is a moon letter, so al- keeps its l — no assimilation here.

sentences.trap: nashrab — the na- is "we", the last prefix of the paradigm, and still no pronoun anywhere in the sentence.
sentences.sound: NASH-rab ash-SHAAY fi l-ma-SAAʾ — the evening ends on the little catch.

variations.cue: I drink tea in the evening
variations.changed: na- → a-: back to I

variations.cue: We drink coffee in the morning
variations.changed: evening tea → morning coffee: both slots swap

variations.cue: We don't drink tea at night
variations.changed: lā in front of the na- verb — the family habit, denied for the night

mistake.display: nashrab ash-shāy fī al-masāʾ dāʾiman kull yawm
mistake.script: نشرب الشاي في المساء دائمًا كل يوم
mistake.why: English can stack "always, every day" for emphasis. Arabic picks one time expression per plain sentence — fī al-masāʾ already carries this one.

sentences.usage: The family habit — na- is the household's prefix.
sentences.mnemonic: masāʾ — evening; you already wish people masāʾ al-khayr with it.
